owner: CC owns the code and the proofs. Akien owns the one bound CC may not touch and it is named here so no build quietly reaches for it: the 5s liveness threshold is RULED, and widening it to make the DEAD flicker go away would be exactly the plaster the 2026-08-14 rule forbids
workflow_and_state: code-seam@v2: THINKME -> TICKETME -> BUILDME -> PROVEME -> WATCHME(the-loop-never-blames-a-device-for-its-own-age) -> PROVED -> [SUPERSEDED]

watchme.trigger: each read over the trouble store. TRUE when a live ground-loop-device-* ticket exists whose device folder imports CLEANLY under a fresh discover() — the exact signature of this outage, cheap to evaluate because it is the same discovery the loop already runs. ONE such ticket fires it: this failure mode is silent by construction, so waiting for n is waiting in the dark.
watchme.enough: NEVER CLEARED BY A QUIET PERIOD — a quiet period is precisely what this outage looked like for 29 hours. Cleared only when a live ticket of this shape has been absent ACROSS AT LEAST ONE OBSERVED LOOP RESTART, the event that creates the staleness. Until a restart has been survived, silence is untested rather than evidence.
watchme.carrier: cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/probes/loop_not_stale.py — carrying the live bench tickets, each device's current discover() verdict, the loop's process start time, and the newest mtime in the cairn tree, so a reader separates 'the loop is old' from 'the device is broken' without going back to disk (I-complete-diagnostic-on-first-pass).
watchme.nexus: triage — the finding is 'a device is benched and imports fine', and splitting a stale loop from a genuinely-fixed-but-uncleared defect from a device broken some other way is a routing question, not a hypothesis about mechanism.
watchme.consumer: harbor_master. It deposits and pokes and carries no authority: the back-edge is the owner's act (Law 6). A fire means compare the loop's process start time against the tree's newest mtime FIRST — that one comparison separates the causes, and getting it backwards is how this went unread for 29 hours.

chart_claim: validate-20260814T153730-54fbdda23d77 — chart chain complete with real content; verdict berthed at verdict-20260814T163532-d7575fd67c39
dependencies: MEASURED, not assumed: the trouble lane already has both doors (raise_trouble / clear with required what_changed) and an append-only occurrence history, and it recorded this entire outage faithfully — it is the only reason the timeline could be reconstructed at all. Nothing in the lane needs changing.

ProbeCache's mtime keying is CORRECT and out of scope: it invalidates the probe FILE properly. What it does not do — invalidate the dependency closure — is the gap, and the fix is a predicate on the failure path rather than a wider cache.
discovery.load_module already execs each probe off its path under a synthetic name, which is what makes the fresh binding (and therefore the identity mismatch) happen; it is correct and stays.
read_liveness and its ruled 5s threshold are read-only here.
filed_edges: THE SESSION-OPEN BANNER SURFACES LIVE TROUBLES AND OFFERS NO WAY TO ACT ON THEM, and no bin/cmd command clears one. Fifteen stale troubles survived many sessions of being displayed. A surface that shows a red with no door beside it trains its reader to scroll past — which is measurably what happened.

NOTHING RESTARTS THE GROUND LOOP. It runs as a bare `python3 -m cairn.devices.ground_loop` from the repo root with no systemd unit, no launcher, and no supervision; the 29-hour-old process was the one started by hand. A heartbeat whose own lifecycle is unmanaged will drift from the code again, and this ticket only makes that drift LEGIBLE rather than impossible.

A PROBE'S TRIGGER HAS NO COST BUDGET AND NOTHING MEASURES ONE. Individual triggers here run 700ms and no gate anywhere reds a probe for being expensive; the 2531 ms total was invisible until the layer was armed.
